Psychology: cultural

Diversity of experience and the relationship between culture and psychological processes.

What it does

Cultural and cross-cultural psychology studies how culture shapes the mind and how people, in turn, create and transform culture. It asks which psychological processes are universal and which vary with language, customs, religion or the way family and work are organised.

Where it works

  • Cross-cultural research and adaptation of tests to other languages and cultures.
  • Mental health care for migrants and refugees.
  • Intercultural mediation in schools, hospitals and social services.
  • International cooperation and global mental health.

What research has contributed

  • Most psychology has been done with "WEIRD" samples: Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic. They are a minority of humanity, and in some respects an unusual one.
  • Self-concept: in some cultures people tend to describe themselves by personal traits and in others more by relationships and roles (Markus and Kitayama).
  • Perception: there are cultural differences in how susceptible we are to some visual illusions, or in whether we attend more to the central object or to the context.
  • Emotions: basic facial expressions are recognised in many cultures, but the rules about when and how to show them vary widely.
  • Distress: psychological suffering is expressed with different words and symptoms across cultures, something DSM-5 addresses with the cultural formulation interview.

An example

Since the 1960s it has been known that the Müller-Lyer illusion, with two equal lines that look different in length because of the arrows at their ends, is not perceived the same everywhere. In a classic study by Segall, Campbell and Herskovits, some populations living in environments with few corners and straight lines were much less susceptible to it than American students. The visual experience of each environment seems to influence how we see.

Why it matters

A test or therapy that works in Madrid will not necessarily work the same way in Dakar or Lima. Taking culture into account prevents misdiagnosis, improves relationships with patients and makes psychology truly a science of all human beings.

References

  1. Henrich, J., Heine, S. J. y Norenzayan, A. (2010). The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 33(2–3), 61–83.
  2. Markus, H. R. y Kitayama, S. (1991). Culture and the self: Implications for cognition, emotion, and motivation. Psychological Review, 98(2), 224–253.
  3. Segall, M. H., Campbell, D. T. y Herskovits, M. J. (1966). The Influence of Culture on Visual Perception. Indianápolis: Bobbs-Merrill.
  4. American Psychiatric Association (2013). Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5.ª ed.), sección III: formulación cultural.
